story_text.value:
The first beta of Hammerspoon 2 is now available! Hammerspoon 2 is a ground-up rewrite of Hammerspoon that uses JavaScript instead of Lua, using the same JavaScriptCore engine as Safari, and it's now the main version of Hammerspoon.

It requires macOS 27 or later and is a separate app with its own config, so you can keep Hammerspoon 1 installed while you try it out. Once installed, it checks for updates itself.

We have a Getting Started guide for new users, and a Migration guide for anyone coming from Hammerspoon 1.

It's a beta, so expect some rough edges. Please report bugs and feature requests on GitHub.

story_text.value:
In short:

For the past few years, I've been building a biohacking platform called Plants Research Pro (PRP), designed to help people discover research on bioactive materials and put that research to practical use. Recently, I added a new feature to PRP which is turning out to be my favorite so far: The Chess Lab. This is essentially a set of tools and protocols for biohacking in chess, some of which you can try right now via the link -- I recommend a Single-Session Experiment, which is a 6-test protocol that lets you explore how some intervention, like coffee, might improve your cognitive function in the context of chess.

-

In detail:

The idea for Chess Lab started about four years ago when I came across research by Prof. David O. Kennedy's group showing that sage, cocoa, and other materials can enhance some cognitive functions. If I remember correctly, the subjects were healthy young adults (possibly uni students). I really wanted to test this on myself, and since I like chess, I chose chess as my 'test platform'. I'm not gonna go into the formulation, but I tried sage alone, sage with cocoa, and sage with cocoa and milk. The third mix seemed to give me the best focus and attention (for about 4-6 h), and my rating started to climb after a few weeks. But there was an issue - I had no idea if I was simply improving naturally, or if the mixture was enhancing it. This annoyed me a little bit, and made me realize that PRP needed an N-of-1 experimentation system.

After finally getting around to it, PRP's Experiments system was implemented earlier this year, while Chess Lab was added about a month ago. Both are now live, although testing and refinement are ongoing. The system also supports N>1 experiments, so can be used with a group of people as well.

There are six cognitive tests and a Single-Session Experiment (SSE) to play with for free. The tests are based on those used in cognitive research, while SSE is a simple before-and-after experiment. i.e., you choose an intervention (coffee, tea, exercise, etc.), complete 6 baseline cognitive tests, apply the intervention (drink your coffee or whatever), then repeat the tests to see what changed -- all within a day (or about 1 h for simple SSEs). The results are exploratory, of course, but I think it's pretty cool that I can now do this myself, at home, without going to a university lab.

But I want to make it much better. The signal-to-noise ratio is difficult to estimate, and there are several sources of error. For instance, a chessboard recall test uses positions from real games, but some pawn structures are much easier to memorize than others. I'm examining two approaches: (1) filtering games by board complexity, and (2) introducing random configurations. The thing with (2), though, is that it's less fun and measures a somewhat different aspect of cognition, but that's a story for another day.

For longer experiments, I've added Chess.com statistics, including move accuracy, rating, opponent-adjusted score, etc. And if you're not sure how to set it up, you can describe what you want in plain language (e.g., 'I want to test if lemon peel can improve my chess') and an AI-powered builder will create a research-backed recipe, design the experiment, assign metrics, and select suitable cognitive tests. AI can also help interpret the statistical results. These full experiments are part of the Premium subscription.

In the coming months, I'll add more cognitive tests, analytics, and some ML capability. Most importantly, I hope to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A new Multi-Session Crossover design (repeated SSEs alternating intervention/no-intervention days, with longitudinal analysis) should help, but there'll definitely be more work needed from different angles.

Anyway, if you like chess and the idea of (safely) optimizing cognitive performance with biohacking, give Chess Lab a try! I'd be very keen for feedback, bug reports, or feature suggestions. Thanks!

title.value: Show HN: Biohacking in Chess – can coffee make you a better player?

story_text.value:
Inspired by both Skyrim and the old Sierra games like King's Quest

Features:

- Playable in the browser on desktop and mobile

- Play by clicking, tapping, number keys, or typing

- Original code-drawn pixel art and synthesised music

- Day and night, snow, and a thaw

- Real-time combat with timed parries

- Six skills that rise by use, with perks

- Five spells and four runewords

- Trading, a forge, and repeatable paid work

- Weight limit for what you carry, and a storage chest

- Map, journal, character sheet, and deeds list

- Two-part main story with two endings

- Eleven side stories

- Valley with eight fable-made places and interiors

- Endlessly generated open country beyond the valley

- Eighteen fable-written scenes to find in the wild

- Three far landmarks

- Walls of rock with passes guarded by enemies

- Vaults under ruined towers

- Autosave plus three manual slots

- No runtime dependencies

Limitations:

- Story inconsistencies

- Mismatches between story/description and visual state

- I'm sure plenty more

I'd absolutely love to have some testers from the HN community!

Hello HN

I made PureSound, an iOS app where you can mix field recordings of rain, waves, fire etc. with any frequency (binaural beat/solfeggio tone) and slow synth music which the app automatically tunes the music to the correct pitch.

If you don't want to mix sounds there's pre made soundscapes to choose from for sleep, calm or focus.

The app is free to use with no ads, no account required and works offline- there is a paid subscription for full access to all sounds in the library.

I appreciate any feedback and suggestions you may have for new sounds/features.

https://apps.apple.com/us/app/puresound-sleep-calm-focus/id6...

If you're not on iPhone/Mac theres a free noise generator which includes white, brown, pink, green noise and a rain sounds player for the browser at puresound.app/#listen-free

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

In 2018 I released a kids’ app called Lexi’s World. It took me four years to make, and I was very proud of it.

Lexi is a little girl who lives alone on a tiny planet. Kids use a keyboard to type the names of animals and plants, which then join her on the planet. The keyboard only lets you type real words that exist in the game, so it’s made for kids who are just starting to get interested in letters and words.

You can type in DOG and a DOG appears, type in BONE and it has something to eat. Type POND, OTTER, REEDS, DRAGONFLY, FROG, FLY, LILY and add another OTTER and you have a nice little pond scene Type GORILLA three times and you get a family to hang out with There is a lot to discover.

It got some critical acclaim and won three awards, including one I’m especially proud of from a group of US librarians. But it never found a foothold, and it never had any commercial success.

Three weeks ago I had Fable 5.2 convert it to JavaScript, and it solved a problem that had plagued me from day one. Because the game takes place on a planet, gravity shouldn’t pull things to the bottom of the screen. It should pull toward the center of the world, so animals stick to the surface. In Unity I ended up using a plugin that used [shader technique] to render a flat, rectangular world as a sphere. I also spent months trying to build a custom gravity system. It drove me to tears, and I had quaternions coming out of my ears.

When I ported it to JavaScript, I just asked Fable to build a custom gravity system that pulls everything toward the center of the world, and it did.

That got me wondering what else I could do. One weakness of the original was that there weren’t enough things to make. The vocabulary was sparse, and kids quickly discovered everything there was. I’ve now added a lot more, and it’s exciting to watch kids discover what must feel like an endless supply of animals, plants, oceans and more. It’s finally becoming what I always knew it could be.

Here’s my problem. I’m fairly sure I’ve made something that’s really fun for kids, but it’s a website, which means it’s played on a screen. In my mind it’s closer to Sesame Street than to Power Rangers, and the parents most likely to appreciate that are probably the ones who don’t want their kids on a phone. That’s fair enough, and I get that this could be a gateway to screen time. Still, plenty of people carefully manage their kids’ screen time, and I think this could be a good use of it.

I have no idea how to promote it, which is why I’m posting here. I’d love for people to play with it and tell me what they think. I suspect some adults will enjoy it too. I think it’s a lot of fun, anyway.

It’s at https://lexisworld.org. It’s free to play for 15 minutes, and then you can buy a week or a month or a forver pass - as one off payments - no nasty subscriptions.

Thanks for any feedback!

P.S. I also had Fable translate the game and used ElevenLabs to voice the new words. I don’t speak most of these languages, so I really don’t know how good the translations are. I’m not claiming the game properly supports them yet. If you speak one of them, please give it a try and let me know how it holds up.

title.value: Show HN: Lexis World – a word game for kids who don't need to know any words yet

A 3D simulation of a vertical lettuce farm I built at a hackathon. It runs entirely in the browser. Two copies of the same farm run side by side one on fixed schedules, one with a scheduler that times harvests from scan data and plans the lights around real electricity prices. In the simulation, the scheduled farm uses about 20% less electricity per kg of sellable lettuce.

story_text.value:
FlightTrack was my iPhone flight tracker from the early App Store days (bestselling travel app for 4 years), and I just rewrote it from scratch.

I first wrote FlightTrack as a side project in 2008. It did really well and I quit my day job and started a company around it that was bought by Expedia in 2010; Expedia retired the app in 2017. By then I had burned out and focused my energy on classical singing, which turns out to mean living in airports. But I missed the app.

This summer I started rebuilding it from scratch, with a design inspired by Paul Mijksenaar's fantastic signage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, and working with Claude to write a server in Go and an iOS app in Swift. In 2008 v1.0 took me 6 weeks of evenings/weekends; now it took about the same amount of time, but thanks to Claude, I ended up with much more functionality (e.g. inbound flight tracking) and was able to try entire design iterations as functional code rather than just mockups.

The data is way more expensive now, so it’s a $59.99/yr subscription, but I’m giving a free year to the first 100 subscribers. I'll be adding lots of features soon but wanted to get this version out for Thanksgiving travel. Let me know anything you want and I'll do my best!

title.value: Show HN: I wrote FlightTrack twice
